#2931. Seven times Jamal Shead looked Kyle Lowry-esque in loss to Grizzlies

The Toronto Raptors may have fallen to the Memphis Grizzlies 118-102 on Monday, but there was a familiar presence on the court that both softened the blow of a loss and boosted hopes for the future.

With Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes, Collin Murray-Boyles and especially Immanuel Quickley out with injury, it was a chance for Jamal Shead to step up. Shead ultimately did so while summoning the spirit of Kyle Lowry.

Here are seven examples of how Shead looked like the Raptors legend during the game:

One thing Lowry was known for – other than his ability to lull opponents into committing offensive fouls – was his uncanny feel for the game. Whatever the Raptors needed at any given moment, Lowry usually dug into his deep bag of tricks to supply it. When Toronto was a horrendous 0-for-6 from the perimeter, it was Shead who hit the team's first three of the game.

The point guard followed that up with two additional threes before the end of the first quarter. Shead's three triples were the only shots Toronto made from beyond-the-arc in the opening frame. Considering Shead entered the contest shooting a career-low 21.7 per cent from the perimeter, it was very "Lowry" of him to transform into a deadly shooter when the moment called for it.

"Me being aggressive is going to add fuel to us," said Shead. "They won't be able to load up on Scottie, load up on Kawhi, load up on IQ."

Shead finished with four three-pointers, the most he's made this season. It's the most threes Shead has made since Dec. 9, 2025 against the New York Knicks.

Speaking of lulling opponents into a false sense of security, a player can't have a Lowry-type game without drawing at least one offensive foul. In the second quarter, while Memphis was in semi-transition, Shead drew an offensive foul on Taylor Hendricks.

After the whistle was blown, and while Shead was on the ground, the point guard enthusiastically pointed the other way. It was easy for those in attendance at the Scotiabank Arena to cheer the blue-collar play. Even for those who don't ever see the sequence, if you've watched the Raptors before, you know exactly what this looked like.

Despite the outcome, it still ended up being one of Shead's best performances as a professional. Shead finished with 20 points on 35.2 per cent shooting. He was two points shy of tying his career-high (22 points vs. the Philadelphia 76ers on Jan. 11 in 2026).

The uptick in usage was obviously due to the Raptors' injuries, but Shead was ready for the call.

"A lot of guys wait for those opportunities and are just ready to play," said Shead. "Obviously those are really important pieces for us…but when they're out, it's just next-man up."

Authoring a career-type game while undermanned is very Lowry-coded.

Lowry's stature may have prevented him from living above the rim during his 20-year career, but it didn't stop him from controlling the painted area – and it didn't matter how much height he was giving up.

On two separate occasions, Grizzlies rookie Cameron Boozer had Shead pinned in the paint. The first example occurred in the opening quarter. Shead leaned his body into Boozer's back, daring Memphis to throw the entry pass. Instead, the Grizzlies opted out.

Later in the game, Boozer received a pass near the basket with Shead guarding him. While Shead's help lurked nearby, Boozer quickly passed to the opposite side instead of taking advantage of his size.

While Shead may be light-years away from reaching Lowry's all-time Raptors assists record – 3,447 to be exact – that shouldn't take away from the fact that he's an excellent table-setter. After setting a career-high in assists (16) against the Milwaukee Bucks on Nov. 6, Shead continued to show his playmaking chops against Memphis. He led Toronto in assists with 11.

It's also the way he got his teammates the ball that mirrored Lowry.

Shead's Nash dribble as he exited the baseline before throwing the lob pass was fun. Later in the game, Shead's dribble drive opened up the lanes and as soon as the Memphis defence committed, he kicked it to the corner for an Allen Graves three. Shead's paint touches and vision also make the game visibly easier for Jakob Poeltl.

"We had a lot of great conversations during the game about where he's going to be," said Shead. "He's very mobile and can kind of handle the ball. He's really smart…it's really easy playing with Jak."

An endless amount of pocket passes, dump-offs and alley-oops allowed Poeltl to have his best game of the season. Poeltl finished with 18 points and eight rebounds.

The only player that might've thrown a better outlet pass as a Raptor than Lowry was Marc Gasol, but Shead definitely added to his resume against the Grizzlies. In the second quarter, Shead corralled a defensive rebound and immediately threw a deep ball to Walter on the break. The play shifted the momentum and brought the entire Raptors bench, including Barnes, off their feet.

"Those guys really want to be out there," said Shead. "But they're really engaged with us regardless if they're out there or not, and that's really helpful."

Later in the fourth quarter, Shead fought through the trees and somehow snagged the defensive rebound. Without hesitation, he launched a perfect outlet pass to Jamison Battle in stride, subsequently leading to an easy two points during a pivotal moment in the game.

Lowry had a knack for coming up with clutch defensive plays, especially when the Raptors were in dire need of a stop. When Graves helped knock a ball loose at the top of the arc, Shead teleported to the ball and rushed down the court for a breakaway layup, sending the home crowd into a frenzy.

Moments later, while getting back on defence, Shead motioned to the bench to ask for a breather. Before the whistle blew, Shead swiped at the ball while Canadian Zach Edey had it under the basket, causing it to go off his leg and out of bounds. As the crowd roared, Shead yelled as he walked back to the bench. The play was ultimately overturned due to a Poeltl foul, but it highlighted just how much passion and bravado Shead brings to the team.

Even while taking on a larger responsibility on the offensive end, Shead is still finding ways to impact the game defensively, just like Lowry.

"The more minutes I've been playing, I've took off the gas a little bit on the defensive side," said Shead. "Once those guys come back, I get to do what I do best and go guard the ball."

#2930. Bengals Tuesday Trenches: Super in Spain, SNF and more

The Cincinnati Bengals won their fourth game in a row on Sunday morning in front of a national audience from Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, Spain, by a score of 34-17.

Now, at 6-2 along with Pittsburgh, the Bengals are set to host the Steelers for what kind of feels like the AFC North title game even though we're only in Week 10.

The Bengals were almost perfect on offense. They scored on six of their eight drives (I'm not counting the last drive in which they could have scored but were able to kill the clock), and four of those scores were touchdowns. Joe Burrow completed 24/29 passes for 271 yards and three touchdowns — two to Tee Higgins and one deep bomb to Ja'Marr Chase to cap off their first drive of the game.

The defense had its moments, but the familiar struggles were there too. In the end, the Falcons' offense just couldn't hope to keep up, even though they seemed to hang around a little, especially early in the second half. Still, it never felt like the Bengals were potentially going to lose control of the game.

Here are some random thoughts on their three-score win before we get into the Steelers game:

Tee Higgins is a monster. He didn't have a ton of yards (32), but he caught two touchdown passes, and multiple passes—including one of those touchdowns—with guys draped all over him. Higgins looks like a man among boys when he catches the ball in traffic.

Ja'Marr Chase is a generational talent. His ability to turn into a running back as soon as his hands touch the ball is remarkable. He breaks tackles like a running back and has 220 yards after the catch so far in 2026. What I'd really like to see, though, is a yards-after-contact stat for him.

The offensive line held up beautifully against the Falcons, who came into Sunday morning's game with 18 sacks and weren't too far behind the Bengals. Burrow was sacked twice, but one of those sacks was much more of a coverage sack than anything to do with the line. If they can continue to protect Burrow like they did Sunday, the offense can break records.

The run game finally made an appearance on Sunday. To be clear, I think Burrow can beat about any defense with Chase, Higgins, and the other weapons he has, but it's hard to win in the playoffs if you can't run the ball. The Bengals were able to kill the clock with a solid running game in the fourth quarter. Chase Brown had multiple explosive runs, including one for 19 yards—a season-long for the Bengals' offense.

Dexter Lawrence. That's it. That's all I have to say.

Okay, a bit more: Lawrence didn't show up on the stat sheet much, but he lived in the backfield and forced Michael Penix into throwing early or on the run. He almost caused an intentional grounding penalty at one point. It's amazing how much one man can change the face of a defense.

The Bengals were unable to sack the quarterback on Sunday. This was their first game without a sack, and hopefully it's their last game. Cashius Howell is on IR, and the Bengals pretty much relied on Boye Mafe and Myles Murphy. Cedric Johnson only played 13 snaps, and Shemar Stewart played just 10. It would be nice to see a little more rotation to help keep the starters fresh.

Regardless of DJ Turner's PFF score, remember the receiver he's covering doesn't get targeted very often.

Money Mac strikes again—good from 57 and 43 yards, and that 43-yard kick in the fourth quarter put any hope of a comeback out of reach for the Falcons.

Speaking of the Falcons, we can credit the Bengals for breaking Atlanta—The Falcons traded Jessie Bates Monday morning.

I honestly don't think it's an exaggeration to say that Sunday night's game against the Steelers at Paycor Stadium is one of the biggest games to be played there in the last several seasons. The Steelers are also 6-2, and with the injuries in Baltimore and the Browns doing Browns things, it's not crazy to think the winner of this game likely wins the division.

The Bengals are not the same team they were that lost to the Steelers in Week 3. The offense is awake and clicking. The defense has its moments, but could use some help. Tuesday (today) is the last day they can make an addition via trade, as the deadline is at 4 PM Eastern. I highly doubt the Bengals make a move, but I also highly doubt they'd trade a first-round pick for Lawrence. Can they pull off another trade just five months after the Lawrence trade?

If there was a time to do it, it's now. The Bengals are in prime position to make a run, and they obviously need a little help, especially on defense, to get things right. They could use depth at cornerback as well as linebacker. They could probably get by without any additions on offense, but adding Jonathan Taylor sure would be cool.

The Bengals are favored by 3.5 points, which is a half point over home-field advantage, and a win would put them at 7-2 with a firm grasp on the division, and a handful of winnable games before they host the Chiefs in a little over a month.

This is where we hoped the Bengals would be at this point in the season.

#2929. 3 takeaways from the Mavericks’ thrilling 125-122 win over the Indiana Pacers

The Dallas Mavericks (7-4) survived a wild one Monday night, beating the Indiana Pacers (3-8) 125-122 in one of their most entertaining games of the season. Cooper Flagg was incredible, finishing with 43 points on 16-of-25 shooting, 10 rebounds, six assists, and three steals, while Kyrie Irving added 35 points on seven made 3-pointers. Pascal Siakam led Indiana with 29 points, nine rebounds and eight assists. Dallas trailed by 10 at halftime, but Flagg and Irving powered a second-half comeback and made enough plays late to escape with the win.

Dallas opened sluggishly and spent most of the first quarter trying to dig out of an early hole. Flagg was easily the Mavericks' best player, scoring nine points with five rebounds, two assists, and three steals while shooting 4-of-6. Kyrie started 1-for-4, Caleb Martin missed both shots, and Dallas shot only 40 percent from the field and 27.3 percent from three. Indiana, meanwhile, shot 55 percent from the field and 57.1 percent from three, with Siakam going perfect from the floor for nine points and Aaron Nesmith hitting both of his threes. Flagg's activity kept Dallas within reach, but Indiana was the sharper team and led 31-26 after one.

The Mavericks found more offense in the second quarter, but Siakam completely took over. Kyrie got going with three threes and reached 15 points, while Flagg continued to create as both a scorer and passer. Walter Clayton Jr. also gave Dallas good minutes, but the Mavericks couldn't string together enough stops to take control. Siakam finished the half with 26 points on 8-of-9 shooting and hit five of his six threes, repeatedly answering every Dallas run. Indiana shot 60 percent from the field and 56.3 percent from three in the half, while P.J. Washington struggled badly at 2-of-10 from the floor. Andrew Nembhard hit a turnaround jumper at the horn to send the Pacers into halftime up 66-56.

Dallas finally flipped the game in the third, and Flagg was the biggest reason why. He scored 14 points in the period, getting to his turnaround jumper, attacking the rim, and making better reads as the Mavericks steadily erased the deficit. Kyrie stayed hot with two more threes, while Washington finally found some rhythm with a tip-in and a three. Dallas also tightened up defensively, forcing turnovers and getting better activity from Clayton and Naji Marshall. Siakam cooled off significantly after torching Dallas in the first half, and Flagg kept pushing late with back-to-back finger rolls to cut the deficit to two. Dallas closed the quarter down just 93-90 after entering it trailing by 10.

The fourth quarter was an absolute blast. Dallas and Indiana traded tough shots, mistakes, and momentum swings to the finish, with Flagg and Kyrie carrying the Mavericks offensively whenever things started to fall apart. It was far from clean, with turnovers, unnecessary fouls, and several possessions that could have swung the game either way, but Dallas kept responding. Every time Indiana landed a punch, Flagg or Kyrie found another huge basket. The final minutes turned into a possession-by-possession fight, and the Mavericks finally made enough plays on both ends to survive 125-122. It was messy, stressful, and probably harder than it needed to be, but it was also one of the most fun wins of the season.

Right now, the Mavericks need to do everything they can to keep Kyrie Irving in rhythm. Kyrie was great again Monday, finishing with 35 points on 11-of-18 shooting while hitting seven of his 10 threes, and it felt like a continuation of everything he started against Brooklyn the night before. Since returning from injury, Kyrie has looked noticeably better when he has been able to stack games together. He came back a little rusty, started finding his rhythm, then sat against Sacramento and looked rusty again when he returned. Now he has played on consecutive nights, and suddenly he looks completely comfortable.

Against Indiana, he was the driving force behind Dallas staying alive long enough to make its second-half run. Every time the offense stalled, Kyrie created something, whether it was a pull-up, a three or a tough finish around the rim. He had 25 points by the end of the third quarter and kept making huge shots as Dallas erased a 10-point halftime deficit. The Mavericks obviously have to be smart with him after the injury, but there is also something to be said for letting Kyrie play when he is rolling. Right now, he has his rhythm back, and Dallas looks completely different because of it.

Somehow, Cooper Flagg keeps finding another level.

Flagg finished with 43 points, 10 rebounds, six assists, and three steals while shooting 16-of-25 from the field, 3-of-6 from three, and a perfect 8-of-8 at the line. He was Dallas' best player early when almost nobody else had anything going, then became the centerpiece of the comeback after halftime. He scored 14 points in the third quarter alone, repeatedly getting to his turnaround jumper and the rim, and he continued making huge plays when the game tightened in the fourth.

What continues to stand out is how comfortable he looks with the game on the line. Flagg does not shy away from the moment or wait for someone else to create. He wants the ball, attacks mismatches, and has already developed an incredible ability to create something when possessions break down. His case for Clutch Player of the Year is only getting stronger because this keeps happening. Dallas needed nearly all 43 of his points Monday, and when the Mavericks needed someone to will them across the finish line, Flagg was right there again.

This is becoming one of the biggest differences between this Mavericks team and what we watched last season.

Monday was exactly the type of game Dallas would have found a way to lose a year ago. The Mavericks were down double digits, had stretches filled with turnovers, missed free throws, and unnecessary fouls, and gave Indiana plenty of opportunities to take control. Instead of folding, they kept answering. Kyrie and Flagg made difficult shots, the defense made timely stops, and Dallas stayed composed enough to survive a genuinely chaotic finish.

Close games are rarely clean, and Monday certainly was not. The Pacers shot 52.4 percent from the field and 42.9 percent from three; Siakam was incredible, and Indiana kept finding ways to punch back. Still, Dallas found a way to win 125-122. This team has the talent to make tough shots late with Flagg and Kyrie, but it also feels like Dusty May has given them more structure and confidence in those moments.

Mistakes and ugly possessions will still happen, but the Mavericks no longer seem to panic when games get tight. They believe they can close, and with Flagg and Kyrie playing like this, there is a pretty good reason for that confidence.

#2928. France blames Iran for supermarket refrigerator cyberattacks, weighs sanctions

France is "not ruling anything out" in its response to October's mass cyberattacks on supermarket refrigerators that the country has blamed on Iran, the country's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Tuesday.

The French government summoned Iran's ambassador Tuesday morning after Paris said Monday that the findings of an investigation laid the blame for the hacks on Shahid Kaveh, an affiliate of the cyber unit of the powerful Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Barrot told radio station Franceinfo that the French government could respond with bans on entering European territory and the freezing of assets of anyone held responsible, as it looks to deter any further malicious acts conducted against the region.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it categorically rejected the accusations made by France, labeling them "baseless and malicious."

"This latest round of allegations — a continuation of previous, repetitive claims — is clearly intended to divert public attention from France's own destructive policies toward Iran and the West Asia region. Such a move is highly irresponsible and contemptible; it is a transparent attempt to tarnish Iran's image and disrupt its relations with other nations," the MOF said in a statement, according to Google translation of the original Farsi.

Remote hacks on around 700 grocery stores over the night of Oct. 11 to Oct. 12 caused refrigerators and freezers to heat up by as much as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).

The soaring temperatures spoiled food and sparked fires, generating tens of millions of dollars in damage. Major French retailers, including Intermarché, E. Leclerc, Carrefour, Monoprix and Coopérative U were targeted.

The Paris Prosecutor's Office is seeking international arrest warrants, Paris chief prosecutor Laure Beccuau said in a statement.

Investigators found use of Farsi and IP addresses pointing to devices in Iran, according to the statement, which added that the attacks were committed to serve a foreign power, in this case, Iran.

The hacks targeted refrigeration controllers supplied by Danfoss and Dixell, with attackers remotely taking control of the equipment through web interfaces and starting unlimited defrost cycles while disabling the safety alerts on sensors designed to activate when temperatures exceed a set threshold, it said.

The French government also said Monday that it would propose new European sanctions against any Iranian entities and individuals involved, and summon the Iranian Ambassador.

"France condemns in the strongest possible terms the unacceptable cyberattacks carried out on its territory by the Islamic Republic of Iran against its interests," France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

"This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory."

"This actor poses a persistent threat to our critical infrastructure. These destructive cyberattacks are unjustifiable, inexcusable, and violate international law," the ministry said.

CNBC has contacted the Iranian government for comment.

France attributes several previous cyberattacks on the country to Iran-based actors, including cyberattacks and "information manipulation campaigns" against the newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the Paris Olympics in 2024. Those led to sanctions in March 2026 against private Iranian company Emennet Pasargad.

More supermarket fridges elsewhere in Europe were targeted in November, with stores across Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Finland, Ireland and Sweden reporting losses.

French blood banks were also affected on Nov. 2 by cybersecurity attacks, the French Blood Establishment said.

Temperature and defrost thresholds at cold storage units used to store blood products and samples headed to healthcare settings and biobanks were "set to excessively high levels," the EFS said in a statement translated from French to English by CNBC.

European leaders and the public have meanwhile been rattled by a wave of hoax bomb threats that have caused dozens of passenger flights to perform emergency landings.

"It feels like this could be a pretty unsubtle message from hostile actors to European governments warning that..[they] have the capability to interfere with critical infrastructure and disrupt essential services whenever they choose," Simon Edwards, CEO of cybersecurity testing lab SE Labs, said in an emailed comment.

"Whether this is an attempt to intimidate governments or preparation for something bigger, it shows how vulnerable our infrastructure can be."

"The lack of basic cybersecurity hygiene is the key factor making these attacks possible, why were these fridges connected to the internet in the first place, and accessible without passwords?"

— CNBC's Emma Graham and Sawdah Bhaimiya contributed to this story.

#2926. Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won't make return in Germany

Kerby Joseph's season debut won't come on foreign soil.

Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said in his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket (WXYT-FM) that Joseph will not play in this weekend's game against the New England Patriots in Germany.

Joseph remains on the physically unable to perform list recovering from a cartilage condition in his knee that has kept him out of game action since last October. He returned to practice Oct. 28, and the Lions have until next week to activate him to the 53-man roster or keep him on PUP for the rest of the year.

Campbell has tempered expectations for Joseph's return, though both he and safeties coach Jim O'Neill said Joseph had a good week of practice last week.

The Lions traded for backup safety Andre Cisco on Monday, Nov. 9, adding him to a position group that includes starters Brian Branch and Chuck Clark, rookie backup Keith Abney and special teams player Christian Izien.

BIRKETT: 10 players Detroit Lions could target for upgrades

"It gives us flexibility," Campbell said of the Cisco trade. "That's what it does do is Cisco's obviously safety, he played nickel, he can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can Branch. We get Kerby back eventually here, Kerby gives you flexibility, you keep him where you need him or move him back and forth."

The Lions (6-2) play two games in five days once they return from Germany, against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Nov. 22 and the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving. O'Neil said last week the team had not determined how to work Joseph back in the lineup once he is activated to the 53-man roster.

Campbell touched on a couple other topics in his weekly interview Tuesday.

Asked about Christian Mahogany's benching last week for violating team rules, Campbell indicated Mahogany has done that multiple times this year.

"That's why I have team rules, that's why we have team rules and we all got to abide by them, and if it's broken multiple times, then you do something about it," Campbell said. "We're on good standing and like I said, the ball's in his court. It'll be good."

Asked how Mahogany has responded since his benching, Campbell said, "Listen, we're good. We're all good. He'll be fine."

"Look, if you say you're going to do something, you better hold up to it or otherwise you're going to lose the respect of people around you," Campbell said. "Because if I'm sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don't do it, I'll immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we're going to do here."

On Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, Campbell did not directly answer a question about whether the Lions are close to making any more deals, like they were two years ago when news of the Za'Darius Smith trade broke during Campbell's radio interview.

"No, we're not going to trade for Za'Darius, and as of right now there's nothing that I've heard in the last 10 minutes," Campbell said.

When asked a follow-up about whether the competitiveness of the NFC North makes it more likely the Lions will make a deal, Campbell said, "Oh yeah, we're going to get ready to go. We're going to have our best game plan in all three phases and we're going to be ready to get after New England's ass. I cannot wait."

The NFC North is the only division with all four teams above .500. The first-place Chicago Bears (7-2) added Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade last month, the Minnesota Vikings (6-2) are believed to be in the market for quarterback help, and the Green Bay Packers (6-3) are expected to get top pass rusher Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL soon.

#2925. Trump says Iran war to end 'fairly soon,' plays down prospects of new strikes

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon," adding that Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington.

Trump told reporters in the White House Monday, after a meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, that "We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon."

"Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump said, citing the destruction of its navy and surging inflation that he said has hollowed out its economy.

Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait would "prefer the status quo" which involves maintaining the naval blockade against Iran and "Operation Iron Gate" — a task force announced on Saturday aimed at preventing Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials — Trump said in a Truth Social post.

He reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to have a nuclear weapon and kept the door open for potentially resuming strikes should circumstances change. "America is 'docked and loaded' and ready to go," he said, though caveating that new strikes were "quite unlikely."

The conflict, now in its ninth month, has driven a surge in fuel prices, hitting nearly every sector of the global economy.

The U.S. had reportedly planned for a potential increase in naval forces in the Middle East in the run-up to the midterm elections, with Trump hinting at escalating the conflict after the results.

The administration has since toned down the war rhetoric after bruising midterm election results that saw Republicans lose both chambers of Congress as voters expressed frustration with soaring living costs stemming from the war.

A diplomat briefed on the Qatar meeting told Axios that Trump told Al Thani that he wanted a deal and would give talks a chance, but could reverse course if Iran does not take the negotiations seriously.

Iran has put forward a two-day proposal to the U.S. via Qatari mediators, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official, demanding lifting of the sanctions imposed on Tehran and a new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington was reviewing the proposal, according to the report.

Iranian officials have disputed that talks with Washington were underway. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, reportedly said that Washington should stop "manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."

Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday on the prospect of de-escalation, extending losses from the previous day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate dropped over 1% to $85.8 per barrel, after sliding more than 4% in the prior session. Brent futures dropped more than 1% to $91.56 a barrel, hovering near 10-week low levels.

#2924. Lakers star makes bold Luka Doncic declaration after he surpasses Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar

Walker Kessler has apparently seen enough.

Just 12 games into the NBA season, the Los Angeles Lakers' new center has already crowned his teammate Luka Doncic the best player in the NBA.

"He's the best player in the league," Kessler declared following the Lakers' 124-114 victory over the Atlanta Hawks on Monday night.

And after what Doncic accomplished, who could blame him?

Doncic's streak of 40-point performances finally ended, but the Slovenian superstar still tormented Atlanta with 32 points, 10 assists, eight rebounds, five steals and two blocks.

Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw during a game against the Atlanta Hawks in Atlanta, Georgia, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

More importantly, he accomplished something neither Magic Johnson nor Kareem Abdul-Jabbar managed twice in a Lakers uniform.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Atlanta Hawks during an NBA game in Atlanta, Georgia, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw during a game against the Atlanta Hawks in Atlanta, Georgia, Nov. 9, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Brunson and Anthony Edwards might have a few objections to Kessler's declaration.

But with the Lakers sitting atop the NBA standings at 10-2, Doncic has something those other superstars don't: the league's best record, and an NBA-best scoring average of 40.1 points per game.

#2923. Trump’s C-SPAN call marks latest surprise post-midterm appearance

President Donald Trump made an unexpected call into C-SPAN's evening broadcast Monday, extending a series of surprise appearances after Republicans' midterm election defeat.

"It looks like we've got a call from the White House," host Mimi Geerges told viewers as Trump joined the debut of "Washington Journal Primetime."

Trump congratulated Geerges on the launch before taking questions on immigration, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Iran war.

Asked what he watches on C-SPAN, Trump said he follows viewer call-ins to gauge public sentiment.

"I like to watch the call-ins because it gives me a little of an indication of where we are," he said.

The unannounced, eight-minute call followed another unexpected appearance earlier Monday, when Trump entered the White House briefing room alongside UFC CEO Dana White. Reporters were summoned so quickly that aides did not have time to attach the presidential seal to the podium, according to Reuters.

It was Trump's first briefing room appearance in 198 days, according to a White House pool report. With the press secretary post vacant, Trump joked about offering White the job, to which the UFC chief declined.

Trump said he had been having "a very bad press day," as he floated White as his next press secretary.

Last Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered substantial midterm losses, Trump also abruptly invited reporters to the construction site of his White House ballroom for his first public event since the election.

Trump spent more than 20 minutes discussing White House construction and renovation projects, including the ballroom's Corinthian columns, marble flooring and the helipad, before turning to the election results during questions from reporters.

When asked whether he regretted how his campaign had ended, Trump distanced himself from the Republican losses.

"If I were on the ballot, we would have won," he said.

Democrats won control of both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 elections, dealing Trump a major political setback and setting up a divided government when the new Congress takes office in January.

Trump has long favored direct telephone contact with the media, including live calls to Fox News programs such as "Fox & Friends" during his first term.

CBS News previously reported that Trump personally arranged one such television appearance, while The Associated Press has documented his habit of contacting journalists directly by cellphone to pitch stories and react to live coverage.

— CNBC's Daniel Mangan contributed to this story.

#2922. Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won't make return in Germany

Kerby Joseph's season debut won't come on foreign soil.

Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said in his weekly radio interview on 97.1 The Ticket (WXYT-FM) that Joseph will not play in this weekend's game against the New England Patriots in Germany.

Joseph remains on the physically unable to perform list recovering from a cartilage condition in his knee that has kept him out of game action since last October. He returned to practice Oct. 28, and the Lions have until next week to activate him to the 53-man roster or keep him on PUP for the rest of the year.

Campbell has tempered expectations for Joseph's return, though both he and safeties coach Jim O'Neill said Joseph had a good week of practice last week.

The Lions traded for backup safety Andre Cisco on Monday, Nov. 9, adding him to a position group that includes starters Brian Branch and Chuck Clark, rookie backup Keith Abney and special teams player Christian Izien.

BIRKETT: 10 players Detroit Lions could target for upgrades

"It gives us flexibility," Campbell said of the Cisco trade. "That's what it does do is Cisco's obviously safety, he played nickel, he can play other things on third down in your dime package. So can Branch. We get Kerby back eventually here, Kerby gives you flexibility, you keep him where you need him or move him back and forth."

The Lions (6-2) play two games in five days once they return from Germany, against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Nov. 22 and the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving. O'Neil said last week the team had not determined how to work Joseph back in the lineup once he is activated to the 53-man roster.

Campbell touched on a couple other topics in his weekly interview Tuesday.

Asked about Christian Mahogany's benching last week for violating team rules, Campbell indicated Mahogany has done that multiple times this year.

"That's why I have team rules, that's why we have team rules and we all got to abide by them, and if it's broken multiple times, then you do something about it," Campbell said. "We're on good standing and like I said, the ball's in his court. It'll be good."

Asked how Mahogany has responded since his benching, Campbell said, "Listen, we're good. We're all good. He'll be fine."

"Look, if you say you're going to do something, you better hold up to it or otherwise you're going to lose the respect of people around you," Campbell said. "Because if I'm sitting in that seat and I say one thing and then I don't do it, I'll immediately lose respect for that person. So we stick by what we say we're going to do here."

On Tuesday's NFL trade deadline, Campbell did not directly answer a question about whether the Lions are close to making any more deals, like they were two years ago when news of the Za'Darius Smith trade broke during Campbell's radio interview.

"No, we're not going to trade for Za'Darius, and as of right now there's nothing that I've heard in the last 10 minutes," Campbell said.

When asked a follow-up about whether the competitiveness of the NFC North makes it more likely the Lions will make a deal, Campbell said, "Oh yeah, we're going to get ready to go. We're going to have our best game plan in all three phases and we're going to be ready to get after New England's ass. I cannot wait."

The NFC North is the only division with all four teams above .500. The first-place Chicago Bears (7-2) added Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jeffrey Simmons in a trade last month, the Minnesota Vikings (6-2) are believed to be in the market for quarterback help, and the Green Bay Packers (6-3) are expected to get top pass rusher Micah Parsons back from a torn ACL soon.

#2918. Victor Wembanyama nearly had a historic 40-point triple-double in just 25 minutes of blowout win over Suns

The Phoenix Suns had absolutely no answer for Victor Wembanyama on Monday night.

And he wasn't even on the court for that long.

Wembanyama finished just shy of a triple-double while leading the San Antonio Spurs to a blowout 122-96 win over the Suns at the Mortgage Matchup Center. But instead of a traditional points-rebounds-assists triple-double, Wembanyama finished just one block short of that mark.

He put up 40 points in the win, and had 11 rebounds and 9 blocks to go with 3 assists in just his 25 minutes on the floor. It would have been the third time in his career that he's logged a triple-double with blocks, following an outing in the Western Conference semifinals last season where he had a NBA playoffs-record 12 blocks against the Minnesota Timberwolves. Wembanyama also pulled off the same feat in 2024, and is the youngest player in league history to do so.

Wembanyama is now just the second player in league history to ever record multiple games with at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and 8 blocks in a single season, joining Wilt Chamberlain. Wembanyama had a similar stat line in a win over the Mavericks earlier this month where he finished with 52 points, 24 rebounds and 8 blocks, which he did in 34 minutes.

According to The Athletic's Jared Weiss, there are only nine other players in NBA history to ever have at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and 8 blocks in a single game. The fewest minutes anyone else has ever needed to hit that mark was 38. Chamberlain is the only other player to do so with less than 20 field-goal attempts.

Since 1980-81, only one player — Sleepy Floyd on Feb. 26, 1991 — scored 40 points in fewer than Wembanyama's 25 minutes, 21 seconds.

Wembanyama was incredibly efficient throughout the night. He missed just four of the 19 shots he took, and had 22 of his 40 points in the first half. That gave San Antonio a 15-point lead at the break.

In the third, Wembanyama grabbed his seventh block and just shrugged his shoulders at Ryan Dunn as the ball went flying out of bounds. He then followed it up with a wild finger roll in which he took off from just inside the arc moments later.

The Spurs didn't need to keep Wembanyama in the game much longer after that. They pulled him early in the final period as they cruised to the 26-point win without any issue.

Before he left for good, it even looked like he was just toying with the Suns. They simply couldn't stop him.

Devin Booker led the Suns with 32 points while shooting 10-of-17 from the field. Khaman Maluach added 11 points off the bench, though they were the only two Suns players to hit double figures. The Suns have now lost five of their last seven games, and sit at 3-6 on the season.

Dylan Harper had 17 points to go with Wembanyama's 40-point outing. De'Aaron Fox finished with 15 points and nine rebounds, too. The Spurs now sit at 9-2 after Monday's win, which marked their ninth straight after dropping back-to-back games to open the season.

Wembanyama is only 11 games into his fourth season in the league, and it's still early November. But he is already making a big statement in the MVP race as the Spurs get the jump in the Western Conference. If Wembanyama keeps this up, they are going to be a very, very hard team to beat in a few months.

#2917. Discussion: What is your dream trade deadline move for the Detroit Lions?

Welcome to NFL trade deadline day. After 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, no more trades can be executed until the start of the league year in 2027.

For the Detroit Lions, that likely means this is their last opportunity to make a roster upgrade for the 2026 season. And while the Lions don't have any massively pressing needs, they are in a bit of an arms race in the NFC. The Chicago Bears added DT Jeffery Simmons a couple of weeks ago. The Seattle Seahawks added guard Quenton Nelson. The 49ers brought back DeForest Buckner.

Detroit is in a good spot in the NFC—currently holding onto the fifth seed in the NFL playoff standings—but just about everyone in contention for a postseason spot is playing decent football right now.

The Lions have already made one minor move before the deadline, trading for reserve safety Andre Cisco. But I'm guessing most Lions fans want more. So today's Question of the Day is:

My answer: Trading for Eagles linebacker Zack Baun.

Philadelphia has already shown a willingness to trade amid their 2-7 start to the season. On Monday, they sent defensive tackle Jordan Davis to the Jacksonville Jaguars for a first-round pick and a future second-round pick. That's a pretty penny to pay, and it may be indicative that Baun will be costly if the Eagles are going to let him go.

But in Baun, the Lions would be getting a dynamic playmaker. Baun does everything in that Eagles defense. He's above average in coverage—grading 71.4 or better in each of the last three seasons, per PFF. He's a pass-rushing threat, with nine sacks since 2024. And he's an absolute force in the run game, as well.

He'd also come with an insanely team-friendly contract, seeing as most of his money is currently tied up in signing and option bonuses that stay with the Eagles upon a trade. Detroit would only be due a prorated version of his $1.215 million salary this year, then they would have an option for 2027 to pay Baun a $14.4 million option bonus to keep him around in 2027.

Now, that low salary would likely mean shelling out significant draft capital to lure him away from Philly. We're likely talking about a second-round pick, minimum. But if that's the price, I'd pull the trigger.

The Lions don't just have questions at linebacker this year—with Jack Campbell's future in football unknown, Jimmy Rolder on season-ending IR, and Devin White also on IR. But Detroit also has questions beyond this year. Only Campbell, Derrick Barnes, and Rolder are signed for 2027, and there's an out in Barnes' contract if Detroit wishes to move on. Baun would give the Lions a head start on fortifying their linebacker room for the future.

#2916. 5 Offseason Question for Pirates at GM Meetings

The 2026 MLB GM meetings are underway in Las Vegas. Typically, these meetings spark offseason buzz and rumors but don't produce much action. Instead, the groundwork for future deals is typically laid this week.

But this year is different. Teams and players are up against a ticking clock as a lockout is expected to take place once the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. The uncertainty surrounding this offseason could spark more aggressiveness and earlier action.

The Pirates have quite a few items on their checklist. Ben Cherington said at the end of the regular season that he will be ready to strike if something comes to fruition before the lockout.

Here are five offseason questions for Cherington and the Pirates.

The $60 million question? The $80 million question? Whatever the dollar amount is, it's by far the biggest question for the Pirates this winter.

It's been over a decade since Pittsburgh had a player of Lowe's caliber reach free agency. Lowe was sensational on both sides of the ball in his first year with the Pirates. He sparked a drastic offensive turnaround by leading the team in home runs and RBI and could win his first Silver Slugger next week. He also turned himself into a strong defensive second baseman.

The Pirates will face stiff competition to try and retain the 32-year-old. Lowe is one of the top free agents available this year and there are a lot of teams in the league have a need at second base. There has been a wide range of contract predictions for what it might take to sign Lowe. But if the Pirates want him back, they'll have to shatter their franchise free agent contract record (three years, $39 million).

The logical option would be to slide Nick Gonzales back to second base if Lowe signs elsewhere. Gonzales was one of seven MLB players this season to bat .300 but struggled defensively in his first season at third base.

But the free agent third base market is not particularly strong. Japanese star Teruaki Sato tops the list, followed by options such as Alec Bohm and J.P Crawford. The Pirates went to the trade market to land Lowe last offseason and it might make more sense to go that route again should Lowe depart. Top trade options include the Astros' Isaac Paredes and the Athletics' Zack Gelof.

If the Pirates did explore a second baseman, there are some solid options available in free agency. Jazz Chisholm Jr., Luis Arraez and Gleyber Torres are among the fallback options.

While most of the attention will be on Lowe and second/third base, the Pirates do have several other needs on their roster.

Topping the list is a left-handed relief pitcher. Mason Montgomery, Evan Sisk, Brandon Eisert and Hunter Barco are the only left-handers on the 40-man. Montgomery, who is the team's closer, is the only option that can be fully trusted. Gregory Soto is a free agent. Maybe the Pirates will think about re-signing him. If not, there are plenty of other options available.

After that, the Pirates should be looking for a right-handed bat to help solve some of their problems against left-handed pitching. A leverage reliever and starting pitching depth are among their other needs.

With talks of a potential salary cap and floor in the next CBA, the Pirates have been a hot topic this offseason. Owner Bob Nutting has developed a reputation as an owner who doesn't spend, and it's impossible to disagree with anyone who has that opinion of him.

The Pirates were more aggressive spending money last offseason than they usually are. They signed their first multi-year free agent (Ryan O'Hearn, two years, $29 million) in almost a decade. They added Lowe's salary via trade and signed Soto and Marcell Ozuna (whoops).

But the Pirates enter this offseason with a payroll that's already projected to be $100 million. That's not far off from their Opening Day payroll this year, which was a franchise record. Pittsburgh is closer to the playoffs than they have been any year in the last decade. Will Nutting open up his wallet to make a legit push?

One way the Pirates can create financial flexibility is by trading Mitch Keller. The veteran right-hander is owed $18.4 million next year and $20.4 million in 2027.

The Pirates flirted with trading him last offseason. In retrospect, they probably should have. Keller not only had his worst season since in five years but ended the year on the IL with a right arm teres major muscle injury. Teams will understandably be reluctant to take on Keller and his contract given what happened this season.

If the Pirates did want to trade Keller, they shouldn't expect much in return other than salary relief. Some other options for facilitating a deal include adding a prospect or other assets or eating some of the money owed to him.

#2915. 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong

A little-noticed category in Friday's blockbuster jobs report is challenging the consensus view about job losses caused by artificial intelligence.

At least for now, the data suggests the U.S. is gaining jobs as a result of the AI boom, not losing them.

And another category suggests the strong jobs numbers could have some staying power.

Nonfarm payrolls grew by 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Friday report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It was a surprising surge in hiring that blew way past Wall Street's expectations. Economists polled by Dow Jones had forecast growth of just 59,000 for the month.

Here are three surprising things you might have missed from the report.

Hiring for consultants surged in the month, sending the profession's total head count to a fresh record.

The labor force for management, scientific and technical consultants expanded by 17,300 jobs between September and October, the largest month-over-month increase in nearly two years. This category is a subset of the professional and business services sector tracked by BLS and accounted for 25% of the entire sector's gains for the month.

What's more, this workforce has grown by more than 45,000 jobs over the past year. That gain pushed the total employee base for these types of workers past 1.9 million for the first time on record, according to BLS data.

Hiring in the industry had largely stalled since 2023 following years of rapid expansion during the pandemic. Wall Street has questioned if the rise of artificial intelligence will curb demand for these services.

Those fears have led shares of consulting firm Gartner to lose more than half of their value over the past three years. Accenture and FTI Consulting have dropped about 18% and 9% over that period, even as the S&P 500 has climbed roughly 74%.

Now, some economists are speculating that the recent jump could be driven by businesses hiring consultants to help them adopt AI. Gartner forecast in September that worldwide AI spending would total $2.7 trillion in 2026, a nearly 50% increase year over year.

"The AI buildout and corporate interests to increase utilization will keep the technical consultants employed," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial.

Roach called the consulting sector a bright spot in October that is "worth watching." He noted that these jobs also saw double-digit growth in the late 1990s, as firms raced to implement new internet technology into their businesses.

So far, data suggests that AI may be adding more jobs to the labor market than it is taking away through automation. An assessment by Moody's Analytics found that AI has created a net 786,000 jobs since ChatGPT launched in November 2022, driven in part by data center construction.

"Wasn't AI supposed to destroy jobs? The most dystopian scenarios even called for mass unemployment," Mark Zandi, Moody's chief economist, wrote in a social media post on Monday. "That risk hasn't gone away, and AI-driven productivity gains could still shift into a higher gear. But for now, AI is adding to job growth, not subtracting from it."

Hiring of temporary workers also drove growth, which could signal that the labor market is heating up.

The subsector's payrolls grew by 18,600 in October, one of its largest month-over-month increases since 2022. This category is another part of the professional and business services sector and accounted for 27% of the sector's gains for the month.

The total size of this workforce is still well below record highs set in 2022. But headcount has grown roughly 3% since December and now sits at levels last seen in April 2025, the month that President Donald Trump's rollout of his plan for steep tariffs put corporate America on alert.

Economists see temporary hiring as a leading indicator in the labor market. Conventional wisdom suggests that companies that hire new workers on a short-term basis often transition them to full-time roles later.

That could be what's happening here, but the fact that the end of the year is approaching makes it harder to tell. The boost could be a result of hiring as the holiday shopping season approaches — and if employers are staffing up for the holidays, they are less likely to retain those workers when January rolls around. Such hiring hasn't typically happened this early, but the season creeps earlier each year. The BLS adjusts its numbers to account for seasonal trends, but won't immediately make an adjustment if the trend is changing.

One hint that holiday hiring may be shifting comes in a separate category of workers: couriers and messengers. This is another area that acts as a barometer for holiday labor demand, and just over one out of every 10 new jobs in the month was in this category.

That category "bears watching for reversal in the months ahead," said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede, a wealth manager.

Hiring related to political campaigns in the final weeks of an expensive election cycle could have also boosted payrolls.

Employment in political organizations has historically spiked heading into midterm or presidential elections, according to a BLS analysis. Staffing levels tend to peak in October of those years, the data shows. Nonfarm payrolls expanded in the months before the 2018 and 2022 midterm elections.

But the vast size of campaign coffers this cycle may have translated into more jobs than before.

The 2026 congressional election is slated to go down in history as the most expensive midterm on record, according to an analysis from OpenSecrets, a money-in-politics watchdog group. Billions of dollars spent on campaigns may have translated into paid gigs that involve door knocking, phone banking or other election-related work.

#2914. Game Recap: Victor Wembanyama scores 40 as Spurs defeat Suns 122-96

What flavor do you like your popcorn? Are you a traditional butter person? Or do you look forward to the holidays, when the Chicago mix makes its annual appearance, and you're treated to that glorious combination of cheddar and caramel popcorn? Because on Monday night against the San Antonio Spurs, you might as well have grabbed a bag of your favorite popcorn, settled into your favorite chair, and enjoyed the show that is Victor Wembanyama.

Coming off an electrifying 52-point performance last week that included 24 rebounds and eight blocks, Wembanyama followed it up with another spectacular showing, this time at the expense of the Phoenix Suns, as San Antonio cruised to a 122-96 victory.

Wemby was the story. Plain and simple. He finished the evening with 40 points on an absurd 15-of-19 shooting, adding 11 rebounds and eight blocks. And here's the part that makes those numbers even more ridiculous: He accomplished all of that damage in a mere 25 minutes of action. You know how we like to track Khaman Maluach's restocks per 36 minutes around here? That wonderful combination of rebounds, steals, and blocks that helps quantify a big man's impact? Well, Wembanyama posted 27 restocks per 36 minutes in this one.

Devin Booker certainly did his part to keep the Suns afloat, scoring 32 points on 10-of-17 shooting from the field. He also added four assists, a steal, and a block while committing zero turnovers. Unfortunately, no other Phoenix starter scored more than seven points to help him out.

Against a team like the Spurs, you need to be able to shoot the three ball efficiently to have a chance at competing, and the Suns simply couldn't do that. They ended 9-of-26 from deep, good for 34.6%. They only turned the ball over 7 times. But they were blocked 10 times.

San Antonio has now won nine consecutive games and sits at 9-2 on the season, while the Phoenix Suns have fallen to 3-6.

The whistle was blown pretty liberally to start the game, as Victor Wembanyama drew three shooting fouls within the first five minutes. San Antonio's early game plan was clearly to attack the basket, knowing the Suns lacked a significant shot-blocking presence on the interior. Meanwhile, Devin Booker once again catalyzed Phoenix's offense, scoring the team's first nine points.

Booker's presence was certainly felt throughout the first quarter, and his impact was evident on both ends of the floor. His best sequence began with a defensive breakup of an alley-oop attempt to Stephon Castle. He then went down to the other end and knocked down a three-pointer over Victor Wembanyama.

Devin Booker finished the first quarter shooting 5-of-8 from the field and 2-of-3 from beyond the arc, scoring 15 of the Suns' 25 points. But the Spurs capitalized on all three of Phoenix's turnovers, converting them into seven points while outrebounding the Suns 14-9. San Antonio took a 31-25 lead into the second quarter.

The momentum carried over as the Spurs extended their run to 12-0 across the two quarters, pushing Phoenix's deficit to 11 points. With Devin Booker taking a breather, the Suns opened the second quarter shooting 1-of-6 from the field and 0-of-4 from beyond the arc through the first 2:37. Meanwhile, the Spurs were a perfect 4-of-4 from the field, including 1-of-1 from deep, and suddenly Phoenix found itself trailing by 14 points.

The Suns were -12 in the non-Booker minutes in the second. From 1:23 in the first to 7:59 in the second, the Spurs put together a 21-2 run.

With 5:19 remaining in the second quarter, the Suns found themselves trailing by 20 points.

Then, with 1:54 left in the first half, Keldon Johnson delivered an unnatural kick on a layup attempt that caught Devin Booker square in the junk, the same type of play that got Dillon Brooks ejected last week. Yet the officials opted not to even review it. Funny how that works, isn't it?

Over the final eight minutes of the half, Phoenix was +3 with Booker on the floor, but the Suns were ultimately outscored 30-21 in the second quarter. Booker finished the half with 23 points.

Meanwhile, Victor Wembanyama had 22 points on 7-of-8 shooting from the field and 7-of-8 from the free-throw line. He also added six rebounds, three assists, and five blocks, leading the Spurs in all of those statistical categories. At halftime, San Antonio led Phoenix 61-46.

The Phoenix Suns opened the second half with a much-needed infusion of energy, finding opportunities to attack in transition and briefly put pressure on the San Antonio Spurs. After an opening three-pointer from Julian Champagnie, Phoenix responded with an 8-0 run to cut the deficit to 10 points. But getting that close seemed to flip a switch for Victor Wembanyama, as San Antonio answered with a 10-4 run of its own to regain control. Before long, the Suns found themselves staring at another 20-point deficit.

Phoenix had another frustrating offensive quarter and again failed to reach 25 points. The Suns collectively shot 8-of-26 from the field and 3-of-9 from beyond the arc, struggling to generate any consistent offensive rhythm. Devin Booker led the way with nine points, while Dillon Brooks contributed five. The rest of the roster? A miserable 3-of-14 from the field.

Meanwhile, San Antonio continued to demonstrate why it's one of the most dangerous teams in the Western Conference. Dylan Harper erupted for 14 points in the third quarter, adding three rebounds and an assist, while Wembanyama contributed 10 points, four rebounds, and a block. Every time Phoenix appeared ready to make things interesting, the Spurs had an answer, methodically dismantling whatever momentum the Suns managed to generate.

By the end of the third quarter, Phoenix trailed 93-68, facing a 25-point deficit and another uphill battle that was becoming increasingly difficult to overcome.

The fourth quarter? Well, the Suns essentially waved the white flag with eight minutes remaining, pulling their starters and allowing Jamaree Bouyea and Rasheer Fleming to see the floor. Cam Spencer, Koa Peat, and Duop Reath followed shortly thereafter, as Phoenix found itself trailing by 30 points and the outcome was all but decided.

There were at least a few entertaining moments from the young guys. Peat, the Suns' rookie, wasted little time making an impression, executing a smooth spin move before finishing off the glass. On the very next possession, he connected with Jamaree Bouyea for an alley-oop, providing a brief spark of energy as Phoenix trimmed the deficit to 26 points.

At that stage, moral victories were about the only thing left to celebrate. Suns lose, 122-96.

The Suns are right back at it tomorrow night as they host the Clippers. We shall see you then.

#2912. Jazz Chisholm Jr. Faces Short Deal Path Like Bo Bichette

Jazz Chisholm Jr. is not going to get the same big money that Bo Bichette secured in free agency last year. Bichette left the Toronto Blue Jays for a three-year, $126 million pact with the New York Mets. The Bichette pact averages out to $42 million per year. The key to that massive contract was the opt-out clauses Bichette added after each season. He could have hit the open market this winter but chose to stay, and he holds that same power again next year. Chisholm now faces a similar path to get his value right, though the market looks much tougher for him.

USA Today's Bob Nightengale wrote a piece on Monday about ten free agents who will draw close attention soon. He looked specifically at Chisholm's situation and the idea of using an opt-out clause. Nightengale wrote that "He could be in for a rude awakening in the free agent market with executives openly wondering if anyone would give him more than a two-year contract." The Yankees did not make a qualifying offer to Chisholm, so he is now a free agent. This means teams can sign him without paying a draft pick to New York, but it also signals the team is ready to move on if the price is too high.

Despite the rough talk from front offices, Chisholm brings real skills to the table. He is a year removed from a 30/30 season where he hit 30 home runs and stole 30 bases. In 2026, he set a career high with 41 stolen bases in 50 attempts. That speed was a bright spot even if his overall hitting numbers were down. He has played second base since the trade from the Marlins and has graded out well there based on defensive metrics. He also has experience playing center field. His talent is undeniable, but teams worry about his consistency over a long term.

Nightengale noted that "No one can debate his talent. He may need an opt-out on any multi-year proposal so he can hit market again and re-establish himself." This strategy mirrors what Bichette did. If Chisholm signs for two years, he can prove he is healthy and hitting, then test the market again for a bigger deal. Various outlets have different guesses on what he might get. According to reports, Chisholm's potential deals are either 3 years/$110 million or 7 years/$185 million. Fangraphs, including Ben Clemens and the median crowdsource, has him at 4 years and $92 million. Kiley McDaniel sees a 2-year, $46 million deal with an opt-out, while MLB Trade Rumors has him at 2 years and $40 million with an opt-out.

The Philadelphia Phillies are one team that might make a move for him. Just Baseball's Ryan Finkelstein forecasts that Chisholm will agree to a two-year, $40 million deal with Philadelphia this offseason. For the 2027 season, Finkelstein stated Chisholm would earn $25 million, followed by a $15 million player option in 2028. Finkelstein wrote that "The best case for Jazz is likely a 1+1 deal where he can reset his market and have a pillow of a player option to fall back on." The Phillies have needed a boost for their offense, and adding Chisholm would give them more power in the middle of the lineup.

Rather than remaining in the American League, predictions suggest Chisholm will join one of this year's National League playoff teams.

#2911. Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing

The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.

There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.

The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.

A week ago here, I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.

In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.

The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.

"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."

This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.

The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.

This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.

The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.

As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.

The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.

Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.

Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.

This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.

But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.

I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.

Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.

So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."

-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast, this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.

-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result:

"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.

"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.

"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

The stampede into perceived defensive stocks has been a crucial driver of Apple shares' massive outperformance over the Nasdaq-100 since the AI-capex agita flared up months ago. Apple heading into Monday's earnings report had outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by nearly 20 percentage points over the prior six months.

Its singular refusal to join the aggressive spending binge to build AI capacity preserved its free cash flow and made it the perfect counterweight to the capex trade, while inflating Apple's valuation to a 15-year high.

But its advantage in free-cash-flow yield has now narrowed, thanks to its stock-price gains and the collapse of peer shares.

#2910. Bilt bets on local businesses, hospitality and major sports franchises, expanding beyond residential rewards

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Bilt is taking its residential property technology out into the neighborhood, announcing the launch of two new platforms designed to help local businesses and event venues attract customers and build loyalty. It is essentially taking the operating system it built for apartment rents and mortgage payments and deploying it across local area businesses, including hospitality, restaurants and sports venues.

The first offering, Neighborhood OS, is an artificial intelligence-driven system that works with restaurants, retail, gyms and other local businesses to attract customers, offer rewards and encourage repeat business. It does this by connecting the business's existing systems, like reservations and payments.

"We're helping local businesses tap into more commerce by being able to reach new customers and accept those rewards as currency to spend," said Ankur Jain, founder and CEO of Bilt. "This is giving every one of those merchants their own Shopify-like platform for real businesses, so now they can run their own marketing campaigns. They can run their own loyalty campaigns."

One example of this might be that a restaurant near a customer's home would offer a perk, then if the customer takes it, the system would recognize that and track that customer to manage future interactions, like more rewards, reservations or guest services. The AI helps the businesses measure which perks worked and which didn't.

Bilt lists initial partners that include Altamarea Group, AM Parking, Lowe's, and Thumbtack. Bilt says it partners with 50,000 merchants so residents can use Bilt rewards at their stores. Businesses that already have rewards systems don't need to replace them. This gives small and midsized retailers an AI platform to use on their own.

They can run marketing offers on their own to drive demand from buildings on the Bilt platform. Examples might be offering a customer a free round of drinks on their 10th visit or pulling in local sports fans by running a watch party on game day. They could push that out through the platform. So merchants now have the same tools that Bilt had to offer its own rewards.

"Offline commerce is six times larger in spend, and it's run by mom and pops, but they have to work across 10 different systems. Everything is done manually for marketing, and there's no way to track what's working," said Jain. "You democratize the ability for now mom and pop to sell against some of the biggest companies online, because they have all those tools."

The second offering is a membership platform for organizations that already have a customer base. That could be sports teams, property companies, hotels and financial institutions. The organization keeps its brand and customer relationship. Bilt layers in additional technology to connect that organization's program with its participating merchants, giving them access to more benefits they don't have through existing programs.

Bilt lists initial members including the Houston Rockets, Phoenix Suns, Sacramento Kings, Related Companies, Hyatt, Constellation Brands and Bozzuto, among others.

"We believe the neighborhood is one of the greatest amenities we can offer our residents," said Toby Bozzuto, president and CEO of Bozzuto. "Through our partnership with Bilt, we have an opportunity to make that amenity an even more meaningful part of their everyday lives."

For professional sports, the idea is to connect fans beyond the stadium. Teams will be able to introduce branded fan experiences that combine loyalty, fan passes, concierge services and neighborhood commerce. This would include rewards at local restaurants, retail businesses and branded events outside the stadium or arena.

Bilt launched in 2021 as a rewards program for rent and mortgage payments. Tenants could earn both loyalty rewards points as well as build credit history. It later expanded into credit cards. It reports 8.2 million members and powers one out of every four apartment buildings, according to the company.
