#2909. San Antonio vs. Phoenix, Final Score: Spurs blot out the Suns, 122-96

In a tale of two (positive) San Antonio (9-2) halves, Victor Wembanyama put his dominant stamp on a 61-46 first half, and second-year guard Dylan Harper shined brightly in a 32-22 third period to inflate a 15-point halftime cushion to more than 30 in the 122-96 win. Instead of doing it over the second and third periods as it did in previous games, the Spurs put up 30+ point quarters through the first three quarters to build and hold its sizable advantage and moved to 3-0 on the road trip.

Wembanyama (40 points, 11 rebounds, and 8 blocks) asserted himself from the tip to put Phoenix back on their heels early on. Harper (17 points, 5 rebounds, and 4 assists) impressed with his smooth stroke and increasing confidence as San Antonio put the game out of reach in the third quarter. De'Aaron Fox (15 points, 9 rebounds, and 6 assists) did the bulk of his damage in the first half. Other double digit scorers included Julian Champagnie (11 points) and Harrison Barnes (11 points), and all Spurs that saw the court tonight again scored.

Devin Booker's otherworldly mid-range shooting (32 points and 4 assists) prevented the Suns from being eclipsed fully in the first half. However, no other Suns joined him in double digits until Khaman Malauch (11 points) did well after the outcome was decided.

Perennial star Booker (nine) was the entirety of Phoenix's offense over the first 5+ minutes. Though they didn't shoot particularly well, the Spurs secured and maintained a slight lead by more conventional means as their outside shots were not finding their mark. Champagnie, in particular, had to find his seeing eye in the paint before knocking down a triple. A seven-point burst by Wembanyama enabled the Spurs to leave the quarter up six.

Wembanyama figured into nearly every part of an opening 10-2 run to start the second period. The lobbing problems – willingness and competency – that plagued prior Spurs squads seemed long gone as the superstar center put up a nearly perfect shooting line from the field (6-6) and line (5-6) only 15 game minutes in. After a couple of free throws, Booker (19 of 38) still had half of his team's output. San Antonio got its lead as high as 20, and more importantly – did not relinquish much of it – as it went to the break up 61-46.

Phoenix found more sure footing on offense to start he third, but the unfazed Spurs executed well in the halfcourt. Harper, in particular, showcased a pair of stepback jumpers, and topped those with a sublime floater on the left baseline to help extend the San Antonio lead to 19. After Harper's fourth and fifth buckets of the quarter, Jacob Tobey noted he "is just in his bag right now." His sixth basket evoked shakes of Michael Jordan's post game. Wemby's 16-foot finger roll capped a dominant third quarter clapback by San Antonio and they went to the fourth ahead by 25.

Fans of the three guard line-up will find a healthy amount of validation in Michael Pina's article today for The Ringer.

Carter Bryant entered action later in the first half and encouragingly willed home a transition three. His second three in the fourth quarter splashed home.

Collin Gillespie's Tough Sequence: In the opening minute of the fourth, Gillespie tried the Steve Nash move on Wembanyama and had his turnaround swatted away, and then his follow-up jumper was deflected, as well. To add insult to injury, the Suns guard was dunked on by Wembanyama at the other end.

Dylan Harper Sequence of the Game: The only thing that prevented him from doing more damage in a 14 point third quarter blitz was twisting his ankle on a Suns foot in transition. All of his field goals in the frame came from different spots on the court, which is very hard to do.

Keldon's Kitchen: That moustache has staying power.

Sequence of the Game #1: In what is a very viable after timeout play late in the first quarter, Fox slithered through the paint and delivered a feathery lob to Wembanyama. On the next possession, Keldon Johnson looked like he left a floater several feet short until Wembanyama took the errant orb and re-directed it through the rim. #greatpass

Sequence of the Game #2: Minutes into the second quarter, Wembanyama appeared to be fooled by a pocket pass from a Brooks pass to Igodaro – only to meet the Phoenix center at the rim to prevent a sure two points, and when Brooks tried to sneak a floater in after an offensive rebound, he, too, was turned away.

Sequence of the Game #3: It only took one possession in the second half for the Spurs to generate another highlight play – this time, Wembanyama found Fox at the dunker spot, and the guard whipped a behind the back pass to the left baseline to Champagnie for a corner three. It's worth watching possibly a dozen times.

Area 51 Sequence of the Game: Wembanyama and Castle orchestrated a beautiful two-man game late in the half that culminated in a Castle one-handed slamma jamma.

Tarris Reed, Jr. (lithe AND bruising big man) playing time: The big man (4 points, 1 rebound, 1 block, and 3 fouls) was an active presence in his eight minutes of playing time.

Fox and Harper scored San Antonio's first two buckets no more than three combined feet from the rim. Castle sand Champagnie put up goose-eggs over the first 5+ minutes, but Wembanyama, Fox, and Harper picked up the slack. Before the viewing audience could blink, Booker had put up 12 of the Suns' 14 points. An Igodaro baseline dunk provided some relief from the Booker scoring barrage. After successive bricks, Champagnie banked home a jumper in the paint to secure his first points. Tshe other Suns started contributing offensively and Khaman Malauch's surprising corner three tied the game. Wembanyama paired two lobs with an encouraging catch-and-shoot three to help San Antonio go up 31-25.

An opening 8-2 burst to start the second put San Antonio up a dozen. Wembanyama's fifth straight bucket – the prettiest to that point – was a baseline fade that Hakeem Olajuwon would have been proud of. After Johnson found Wembanyama for yet another lob, Sean Elliott exclaimed "What a change! Our guys have really figured out that lob!" Wembanyama then turned away Phoenix's lob attempt at the other end. Even after his first miss, Wembanyama snared the rebound and threw down a thunderous two-hand jam. Booker's next field goal caused Mitch Johnson to call a Pop-like timeout. Champagnie and Luke Kornet found each other on consecutive possessions to keep the lead near 20. Phoenix took advantage of the Spurs' hyper-aggressive perimeter defense to get cheap offense at the charity stripe. Booker took a shot to the nether regions on a Johnson bankshot that could be felt several states over. San Antonio ended its well-played half up 15.

A pair of triples from Champagnie and Fox prevented a tough third quarter start for San Antonio. Booker hit the 30 point mark 3 1/2 minutes in, and yet, the Spurs added to their lead. During one possession, Fox, Castle, and Harper occupied the left side (with Champagnie deep in the right corner), which allowed Wembanyama to go back door for a reverse lob from Harper. #2907. FIA boss looks to ‘end age limits’ for office holders – six months after ditching term limits

Mohammed Ben Sulayem is reportedly looking to end age limits for FIA office holders – just six months after the FIA president ditched term limits for those in leadership posts.

Emirati executive Ben Sulayem, 64, has been FIA president since December 2021 and was re-elected last year after other candidates were prevented from standing, due to quirks in the FIA statutes which meant the only prospective vice-president in one region was already aligned with Ben Sulayem.

Currently, FIA statutes rule out anyone over the age of 75 from standing for a presidential term. This rule was implemented in 2024 to "modernise the governance of the FIA and ensure that candidates for the presidency are more aligned with current leadership practices."

Yet just six months after Ben Sulayem ended term limits for those in leadership posts, the BBC reports that Ben Sulayem wants to discontinue the age-limit rule and put forward a proposal detailing as such to the FIA's General Assembly in Shanghai next month.

An FIA spokesperson told The Independent: "An age limit excludes candidates solely on the basis of their date of birth, regardless of their experience, expertise, or ability to contribute. Ultimately, the competent FIA bodies will retain full authority to elect the officeholders they deem appropriate."

"The proposal to remove age limits for FIA officeholders is one of the proposed amendments to the FIA Statutes to be put to the General Assembly in Shanghai in December. It was approved by the World Councils for submission in line with the process set out in the FIA Statutes, and will only take effect if the General Assembly votes in favour."

Ben Sulayem had originally introduced an upper age limit of 70 in 2023, in a move widely seen to prevent Motorsport UK boss David Richards from running.

Ben Sulayem, who is a regular in parc ferme and on the podium after F1 races, has overseen controversial moments in his near-five years in charge.

Ben Sulayem has clashed with Max Verstappen in the past (Getty)

His first term saw Ben Sulayem clash with Lewis Hamilton over the Brit's desire to wear jewellery in the cockpit, while he also angered drivers, including four-time world champion Max Verstappen, for issuing fines for swearing.

Last April, Robert Reid resigned as deputy president for sport, accusing the governing body of a "breakdown in governance standards." And presidential candidates such as Tim Mayer and Laura Villars were unhappy after they could not oppose him in last year's presidential elections.

FIA rules dictate a vice-president candidate must be nominated from each of its six global regions; Bernie Ecclestone's wife, Fabiana, the sole South American candidate, supported Ben Sulayem.

Meanwhile, Ben Sulayem has also voiced his support for end-of-season races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi to go ahead. A final call is expected on Tuesday.

#2906. Polymarket says annualized revenue has topped $1.8 billion

Prediction market platform Polymarket has surpassed $1.8 billion in annualized revenue, the company told CNBC on Tuesday.

That's up from June, when Polymarket disclosed that its annual revenue run rate was north of $1 billion, following the launch of its domestic exchange in May.

Polymarket's revenue is being fueled by growth in that U.S. exchange, which operates as a separate trading venue from its decentralized finance international platform. The domestic exchange saw more than $14.5 billion in notional volume in October, up from $4 billion in June, according to data analytics platform TickerTracker.

That increase has been driven by a series of highly traded events, including the FIFA World Cup over the summer and the start of the NFL season in September. Volume has been supported by the growing popularity of Combo event contracts, which work similarly to sportsbooks' multi-leg parlays, accounted for more than 70% of volume traded on the platform on Sunday.

The revenue growth since June also comes after the company began a fresh $1 billion funding round that values Polymarket at $21 billion.

Polymarket still faces near-term headwinds, though. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is conducting a broad investigation into the company, with questions surrounding advertising practices and whether the company in the past violated a settlement with the agency to bar U.S. residents from accessing its international exchange.

The company also may face increased scrutiny from a Democratic congress, partially due to the position of President Donald Trump's son — Donald Trump Jr. — as an advisor to the company.

But Polymarket previously told CNBC it would work with lawmakers as they begin to understand the growing prediction market industry. "We welcome scrutiny," a spokesperson said.

#2902. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit

The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.

Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.

Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.

"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."

Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.

The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.

Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.

President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.

The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.

Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.

Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.

One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.

"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.

Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.

In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.

"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."

MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.

"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

#2901. Bridgepoint sees opportunity in 're-rated' real estate

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Alts newsletter, a guide to the fast-growing world of alternative investments, from private equity and private credit to hedge funds and venture capital. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

While higher interest rates are chasing many investors away from real estate, Bridgepoint Group sees growing opportunity in overlooked corners of the property market, according to company executives.

With $125 billion in assets, London-based Bridgepoint has expanded from core private equity and private credit into infrastructure, secondaries and real estate. This summer, it announced the acquisition of Kayne Anderson Real Estate, the real-estate investment firm with over $22 billion in assets.

In an interview with Inside Alts, Bridgepoint CEO Raoul Hughes said the acquisition gave the firm a "category-killing" real-estate offering as well as a bigger foothold in the U.S.

"All the products we have are the go-to products within their niche," Hughes said. "They're very entrepreneurial, very alpha-driven and we're all about real value-added investing. What we didn't have prior to coming together with Kayne Anderson was the real-estate piece."

Higher interest rates have created a new headwind for many real-estate funds. Funds that poured money into commercial and residential real estate in 2021, when interest rates were near zero, are now grappling with higher borrowing costs, compressed valuations, slower transaction volumes and more defaults.

Al Rabil, CEO and Co-Founder of Kayne Anderson Real Estate, said higher rates will lead to a shake-out in the industry. Disciplined investors with strong sector expertise will find new opportunities in the fallout, he said.

"People say 'oh interest rates up, real estate bad,'" Rabil said. "It's actually not quite that simple. Yes, interest rates are up, cap rates up, asset valuations down. But this is a longer duration investment business so it isn't day-to-day or quarter-to-quarter. When you get in an environment like the one we're in, it actually produces a very outsized investment opportunity because we're in very rarified air."

Rabil cited three real-estate sectors as being attractive for Bridgepoint and Kayne Anderson. Medical office space will continue to be an outperformer as the population ages. He said the asset class hasn't been below 90% occupancy in over 20 years, with demand far exceeding supply.

He said Kayne Anderson focuses specifically on the higher-margin sub-sectors of oncology, neurology, cardiology and diagnostics.

"People age 65 or over need seven times more doctor visits than those 45 and under," Rabil said. "So the population has a massive need for increased health care that has to be satisfied through medical office."

Another attractive sector is so-called "small-bay industrial," or commercial space used by small businesses and e-commerce retailers.

"Small businesses are 47% of GDP," Rabil said.

When it comes to residential, Rabil said higher interest rates could cause a reckoning. Investors poured billions into multi-family real estate in 2021 and 2022, with many of those loans financed with a 10-year Treasury at around 1%.

"Much of that debt is coming due today," he said. "There is a huge opportunity for very good assets that are structurally broken, in terms of the capital structure."

Hughes said that higher rates aren't likely to impact Bridgepoint's broader portfolio companies in private credit and private equity. He said the firm focuses on high-growth, high-margin businesses that are more resilient to interest rate swings.

"You'd rather rates were stabilizing where they are rather than going up," Hughes said. "And I think rates probably are stabilizing. But from an investing perspective, I don't think it materially damages our ability to drive returns from our equity portfolio."

The Inside Alts newsletter with Robert Frank and Leslie Picker is your guide to the fast-growing world of alternative investments.

#2899. Jesse Minter puts Ravens' identity under review after 4 straight losses

The Baltimore Ravens have reached a point in the season where changes may be coming. After a difficult stretch, head coach Jesse Minter and his staff have taken more time to evaluate what needs to improve, including personnel, playing time, and the team's overall identity. The evaluation comes as the Ravens prepare to face the Los Angeles Chargers on Monday night. Minter hasn't announced lineup changes, but his message leaves little room for assuming the current approach is sufficient. Baltimore needs its identity to show up in its execution, discipline, and consistency across all three phases.

Minter made it clear that the focus isn't simply on making changes for the sake of making changes. It's about figuring out what the Ravens need to do better and making sure the team plays with a consistent identity.

When asked about the team's self-evaluation during the extra time away from the field, Minter explained what he and his staff have been looking at.

"I appreciate you guys being here. We were able to take advantage of the extra time [of] really looking at ourselves in a self-analysis, self-scout mentality over the last few days. What can I do better? What can we do better as coaches? What can we do better as players? Then, when it comes to scheme, who we're asking to do what, playing time, who do we have in the lineup – I mean, kind of everything, I would say. And now as the guys come back tomorrow, we'll give a little bit of a reset to where we're at with the guys tomorrow. We'll be in a race to improve this week."

The Ravens have struggled to put together consistent performances, and Minter knows the team needs to establish an identity that shows up when it matters most.

When asked whether fans should expect significant lineup or schematic changes following the reset, Minter emphasized the importance of making sure the team's identity matches what the coaching staff expects.

"I think that's for our team. But, I definitely feel like a couple days gives you a chance to really look and really dig deep. I think first and foremost, making sure that the identity that we talk about that we want is not just talk. Sometimes that can get lost as you're racing each week to try to get a game plan in and do things. I'm excited for us to sort of re-establish our identity. [With] lineup changes, I think those are all [on an] individual basis. But there's certain things that we have to have really high standards for. So, we'll see how it all shakes out."

Minter isn't promising wholesale changes, but the message is clear. The Ravens have to be better, and the extra time gives the coaching staff a chance to evaluate what went wrong. Now it's about putting those changes into action and finding a way to get the team back on track.

#2898. Amazon's Ring unveils flying drone and robot to patrol homes and businesses

Amazon's Ring is going deeper into surveillance with an indoor drone for home monitoring and an autonomous robot designed to patrol businesses.

The company on Tuesday unveiled the $250 Ring Drone Cam, a security camera that can fly from room to room, including upstairs, as well as capture footage during the day or at night. When an alarm or sensor on windows, doors and home security devices is triggered, the textbook-sized drone travels a pre-set path to investigate suspicious activity. Users can also deploy the drone at any time, the company said.

At a demo in New York on Monday, Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said the drone could be used as a home monitoring tool and as a crime "deterrent" due to the device's built-in LED lights.

"If someone is going around your house at night, and your motion detector goes off on your Ring doorbell, imagine if you see spotlights and something flying across the window," Siminoff said. "You're probably not going to go into that house."

The drone, which can fly up to eight minutes at a time before autonomously returning to its charging dock, has two plastic-encased propellers that emit a loud buzz when it's airborne.

Ring devices have provided Amazon another avenue to grow its presence in the smart home beyond its Echo smart speakers and Eero routers, expanding in a market that Grand View Research estimates will top $200 billion in sales this year. It's equally fertile ground for Amazon rivals Apple and Google.

Ring first previewed its drone, then called the Always Home Cam, in 2020. Siminoff said he chose to hold off on releasing the device until Amazon could perfect the design, sensors and data processing.

The company on Tuesday also debuted the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam. The device repurposes Amazon's Astro home robot, which had a short life as a business device and has seen few upgrades since its 2021 debut, for companies to patrol offices, warehouses and other workspaces.

Ring said it "leveraged the best of Astro" to build the Ring Rover Cam, which it describes as a "purpose-built security robot."

Similar to the Astro, the device is a display mounted on a two-wheeled base with an extendable periscope camera. It also features a "built-in siren," two-way audio and a "light tower" that shines onto the ceiling to help users keep track of its whereabouts.

Siminoff said in an interview that the drone and the robot allow users to monitor multiple areas of their home or business with just one device.

"People like indoor cameras, but they don't necessarily want them everywhere around their home," Siminoff said.

Siminoff said the drone can't fly outside per Federal Aviation Administration regulations, which restrict operating drones unless they're within a line of sight of a pilot.

"We have told our customers not to do that because it's illegal," Siminoff said. "We've also put guardrails in there to make it so it doesn't fly outside."

The Ring Drone Cam ships in the U.S. on Jan. 27, pending approval from the Federal Communications Commission, while the Ring Rover Cam will begin shipping to users on Dec. 16, the company said.

#2896. How much you can make in 2027 and still pay 0% capital gains tax

The IRS has released the capital gains tax brackets for 2027, which include a six-figure earnings limit for the 0% rate for married couples.

If you're eager to sell profitable brokerage account investments, higher income thresholds for the 0% rate could help reduce your tax bill, experts say.

"The 0% capital gains bracket is easily one of the most overlooked strategies for tax-free income," said Stephen Maggard, a certified financial planner with Abacus Planning Group in Columbia, South Carolina.

But it's important to know how the tax brackets work and the possible trade-offs before selling investments.

Despite recent stock market volatility, many investors have portfolio gains after years of market growth. As of market close Nov. 9, the S&P 500 was up about 10% year-to-date. The index also returned more than 16% in 2025, and over 23% in 2024.

If you're planning to leverage the 0% capital gains bracket in 2027 to sell or rebalance brokerage account assets, here are some key things to know.

The capital gains brackets — with rates of 0%, 15% or 20% — apply to assets owned for more than one year, known as long-term capital gains. By contrast, investments held for one year or less are short-term gains, subject to regular income tax rates.

Your rate depends on taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income, or AGI. Taxable income also includes any gains from investments that year.

The standard deduction will rise to $16,600 for single taxpayers and $33,200 for married couples in 2027.

For example, let's say a married couple's AGI is $130,000 for 2027, including capital gains. After subtracting the $33,200 standard deduction, their taxable income would be $96,800, which falls below the 0% threshold.

However, taxable income should include mutual fund distributions, which can "dramatically alter year-end planning projections" and increase taxable income, according to CFP Jim Guarino, managing director at Baker Newman Noyes in Woburn, Massachusetts. He is also a certified public accountant.

If your federal taxable income is above the 0% threshold, you'll pay 15% on the portion of investment gains that exceed the 0% limit, up to that bracket's cap. Gains above that may be taxed at 20%.

Also, the 0% capital gains bracket applies to federal taxes, but your profits could still be subject to state-level taxes, experts say.

As income limits rise for the 0% capital gains bracket due to IRS inflation adjustments, more investors could have tax savings opportunities, experts say.

"There is tons of planning to be done here," especially for early retirees with lower income, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

One strategy, known as "tax gain harvesting," is selling profitable brokerage account assets during lower-income years to leverage the 0% bracket, he said. Keep in mind, these sales stack on top of your other earnings, which could bump taxable income above the 0% threshold.

You can also sell the asset and immediately rebuy it to "reset the cost basis," or original purchase price, said CFP Charles Sachs, chief investment officer of Imperio Wealth Advisors in Coral Gables, Florida.

By resetting the cost basis to current market value, you can reduce future capital gains to trim your tax bill.

When selling assets at a loss, the "wash sale rule" blocks tax-loss harvesting when you rebuy a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale. But the same rule doesn't apply when harvesting gains.

Managing capital gains is only one part of yearly tax planning, according to Guarino with Baker Newman Noyes.

Before selling investments, you should know how boosting AGI could impact your broader financial plan, including income phase-outs for various tax breaks, he said.

For example, modified adjusted gross income can impact a range of tax benefits, such as Affordable Care Act health insurance premium subsidies, which can disappear once earnings exceed the federal limits by even a single dollar.

Another example is President Donald Trump's temporary $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction, which is worth up to $12,000 for married couples per year through 2028.

#2894. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2891. Trump's 2028 successors are already fighting over who to blame for GOP midterm wipeout

Republicans are still reckoning with a historic midterm wipeout, but the fight to assign blame and inherit President Donald Trump's political movement is already underway.

Vice President JD Vance faults the war in Iran. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defends it. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis says Republicans fought the wrong battles. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, argues the party lost touch with voters' economic struggles.

The competing visions from potential presidential contenders offer an early glimpse of the Republican infighting ahead of 2028. But all face the same dilemma: How to convince voters the party can change course without alienating Trump or the MAGA base they need to win the nomination.

The biggest obstacle may be Trump himself, who has shown little appetite for a political retreat.

On Monday, Trump made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room, declaring the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" while maintaining that the U.S. remains prepared to resume strikes. Earlier that day, he questioned the legitimacy of Republicans' midterm defeat, suggesting without evidence that voting machines were responsible, days after saying that after years of election denial, he would accept the 2026 results.

Since the election, Trump has also replaced Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller and backed Republican National Committee Chairman Joe Gruters against a challenger demanding an accounting of the party's losses.

Trump is also keeping his would-be successors guessing. In a CBS interview Sunday, he praised Rubio alongside Vance but suggested he might stay out of the 2028 Republican primary.

"Maybe I'm better off not getting involved," he said, while emphasizing the weight his endorsement could carry.

That dynamic leaves Vance in a precarious position. Entering the midterms as the clear political heir, Vance now faces a critical question: Can he inherit MAGA without inheriting the blame for Trump's presidency?

In a lengthy post on X Wednesday as election results were still trickling in, Vance challenged Trump's initial explanation for the Republican defeat.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, arguing voters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 abandoned Republicans in 2026 over Iran.

Pointing to foreign policy allows Vance to criticize a defining administration decision without repudiating the broader MAGA movement, while echoing his longstanding opposition to foreign interventions. Vance also has national name recognition and donor ties to help his prospective candidacy.

But the election results complicate Vance's argument.

Just 34% of House voters called the war crucial to their vote, versus 49% citing the cost of living and 55% government corruption, according to the CNBC Voter Poll – suggesting a broader backlash against the Trump administration that Vance has spent nearly two years defending.

"You can't campaign against a war from within an administration you serve," conservative commentator Joel Pollak wrote on X, questioning how Vance could distance himself from a conflict he had publicly defended.

In his CBS interview, Trump said he did not disagree with Vance's assessment and acknowledged the vice president had discussed the post with him beforehand. But he insisted the decision to attack Iran was right and suggested Vance also has losses of his own to explain.

After Vance spent months fundraising and campaigning as Republican National Committee finance chairman, Democrats won both marquee races in his home state of Ohio. Amy Acton defeated Vance ally Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, after the vice president defended a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown claimed Vance's former Senate seat, defeating incumbent Republican Jon Husted.

Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., stated Sunday he would not support Vance in 2028 due to his war criticism, calling it a betrayal of Trump. "You have to be loyal to those people who brought you to the dance," Fine said in an interview with LiveNOW from FOX on Sunday, naming Rubio and Cruz as alternatives.

Rubio is making a different bet: Defend the Iran war while distancing himself from the Republican defeat.

"Sometimes, when you do the right thing, you don't know whether it's popular or not, but it's still the right thing to do," Rubio told reporters Sunday before departing for France.

Rubio, who has denied he plans to run in 2028, largely avoided the campaign trail and has stayed out of the immediate blame game. But his dual role as secretary of state and national security advisor ties him directly to Trump's foreign policy record, which could face renewed scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House. The House may vote this week on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a rebuke of the Trump administration's foreign policy.

DeSantis, who is not in the Trump administration, is questioning the party's entire playbook.

The outgoing Florida governor called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event" for Republicans at a news conference Wednesday in Tallahassee, Florida, accusing Washington of failing to deliver on its promises while fighting culture wars that no longer resonated with voters.

"Republicans ... really were fighting yesterday's battle," DeSantis said at the news conference.

It was a striking critique from a governor who built his national profile on those same fights.

DeSantis can point to Republicans' ability to retain control of Florida even as Democrats flipped longtime GOP strongholds elsewhere. But Republican Byron Donalds won the governor's race by just 1.3 points, while Democrats gained ground in the Legislature.

Still, Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., credited DeSantis with building a "massive sea wall against the blue tsunami" in an X post.

The scramble to succeed Trump extends well beyond Vance, Rubio and DeSantis.

Cruz called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation" in a post on X Wednesday, blaming Trump's tariffs and the prolonged Iran war. Other potential 2028 contenders include Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders and former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin, who face the same challenge of moving beyond Trump without alienating his base.

Some wealthy Republican donors are already looking beyond Vance, weighing DeSantis and other alternatives amid concerns that a candidate from Trump's administration would inherit the political baggage of his second term and low voter approval ratings.

The divisions extend to Trump's own coalition. Among voters who backed Republican House candidates, roughly two-thirds of those under 30 approved of Trump's performance, much less than the nearly nine in 10 voters 65 and older, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. Younger Republicans were also more skeptical of the Iran war and U.S. support for Israel, according to the exit poll data.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance said Wednesday. "Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost."

#2890. Managerial 'inconsistency' hurting Ghana - Hughton

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton reveals cancer diagnosis

Ex-Brighton boss Hughton backs mental health drive

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 Afcons under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right) [Getty Images]

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

Coventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June [Getty Images]

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's Afcon in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests of the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

*Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards

#2888. FDA warns of vision loss risk linked to popular GLP-1 drugs like Wegovy, Zepbound

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is requiring new safety warnings on all GLP-1 drugs after finding evidence of a potential increased risk of a rare eye condition, the agency said on Monday.

The condition, which can cause sudden vision loss, known as nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), is rare, and a causal relationship has not been established.

The FDA is requiring the makers of all GLP-1 medications to add a warning about the potential increased risk of NAION associated with use of these medications, it said.

NAION is a condition that can result in sudden decreased vision, including permanent vision loss. It is caused by decreased blood flow to the front part of the ​optic nerve — the underlying cause is not completely understood, however.

NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 products, the FDA said.

Ozempic and Wegovy maker Novo Nordisk said it "continues to believe the data do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, and we remain confident in the benefit-risk profile of our GLP-1 medicines."

CNBC has reached out to Eli Lilly, the company behind Mounjaro, Zepbound and Foundayo, for comment.

The FDA decision follows a review of clinical trials, real-world patient data, and published studies.

An analysis of 126 trials involving more than 134,000 patients found 6.4 cases of NAION per 100,000 patient-years among GLP-1 users, compared with 3.8 among patients receiving other treatments or placebos.

Several observational studies also identified an increased risk, supporting the FDA's concerns.

The FDA's class-wide labeling action is "likely to attract attention but should have limited impact on GLP-1 uptake," according to Citi analysts.

It may temporarily increase patient and investor concern, but the rarity of NAION and substantial weight, glycemic, cardiovascular, renal, and sleep apnea benefits should preserve a favorable benefit-risk profile and limit changes to prescribing the medicines, they added.

While GLP-1 drugs have been shown to lead to benefits beyond weight loss and controlling blood sugar levels, many also carry the FDA's strongest safety warning, known as a boxed warning, over a potential risk of thyroid tumors.

Studies have shown that semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy and Ozempic, and tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Mounjaro, cause thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents. It remains unknown whether the drugs cause these tumors, including a rare form of thyroid cancer, in humans.

#2885. Broncos at Panthers: The No Bull Review

The phrase I kept hearing heading into this game was the dreaded "trap game." This plucky Carolina Panthers team was supposed to catch the Denver Broncos napping as they look forward to their bye week after a grueling game with the Kansas City Chiefs.

Rest assured, Broncos Country, that this Broncos team does not overlook anyone. The Panthers fired their former defensive coordinator, Ejiro Evero, leading up to this game. They added some tweaks to their defense. They have a seriously talented quarterback in Bryce Young.

All to no avail. The Broncos adjusted. They adapted. They overcame all obstacles. It is just who they are and what they do.

This was a hell of a win for the Broncos. Losing both Jaylen Waddle and Riley Moss was rough. While the offense did a good job of staying on track, the defense was honestly shook with the loss of Moss. It completely changed how the defense played, which led to the defense needing to rely on turning the ball over more than playing consistent, effective defense like we are used to.

Week after week, this offense continues to evolve in a positive direction. The passing game looked arguably the best it has all season (granted it was against a very dinged-up secondary).

The run game had significant trouble being a focal point against the Panthers' tenacious front. They made do and made plays in fits and spurts on the ground while mainly leaning on Nix's arm to do the bulk of the offensive work.

The playcalling this week was honestly some of the best I've seen all season. I personally would like to see a more balanced approach, but that wasn't going to work this week against this opponent.

It was refreshing to see a matchup like this where there's an obvious weakness in the defensive secondary that the Broncos fully took advantage of. Sean Payton started the game wanting Nix to attack the secondary, and that never changed until it was time to turtle up and run the clock.

Bo Nix sure did respect the position of quarterback in this game (AMARITE, Ditzpatrick!?). He went downfield early and often in this game with air yard numbers that would make Patrick Mahomes cry (still waiting for the talking heads to start wondering if Mahomes is washed with how short his throws are lately).

He did throw another boneheaded pass where he decided the route he was throwing immediately and was completely oblivious to the underneath defender that earned him an interception. Outside of that, I thought he played a superb game.

What I liked most about Nix in this game was how often he was looking off defenders to set up his passes. What's cool about this is that it not only manipulates the defenders, but shows how much he's getting in sync with the receivers and knows where their routes are. He was impressively quick on the trigger a couple of times during these look-offs.

The biggest thing causing this offense to look clunky is the line. Ben Powers was practically a turnstile on more than a few plays. Luke Wattenburg had a couple of head-scratchers. Mike McGlinchey just got beat multiple times (he got spun backwards on one play I saw that had me seeing visions of Ty Sambrailo).

The front for the Panthers won the day from what I saw throughout the game. It honestly had me wondering if they changed up how they were playing vs. what Evero had them doing previously. I'd be curious to know what Panthers fans who know the game would have to say on this…hit us up in the comments. Is your front just that good, or did they change things up?

Jonah Coleman rightly took over the starting duties this game and emerged as the #1 RB on the team. With the line having so many troubles, he wasn't producing what we would like to see. He was able to cook with what he was given, though. He showed impressive burst and speed on his touchdown run around the edge. He was also very effective as a receiver out of the backfield with 4 catches for 31 yards. The fumble late in the game was very tough to see. I feel like he and Nix will both need to work their pitches during the bye week to shore that up.

JK Dobbins made an excellent cutback and jump step to gain 11 on his first run. He only got 4 carries on the day total, with his other 3 gaining only 7 yards.

Welcome back, Pat Bryant! Our young rock star of a receiver got a 12-yard gain on his second catch off a crossing route. He caught an 11-yard pass to move the chains in the 3rd quarter. Bryant benefitted from blown coverage for the easiest touchdown he will ever catch late in the 4th quarter for 26 yards.

On one hand, Courtland Sutton led the team in targets and was a big focus for the offense. On the other hand, they missed 4 of his targets. He is cash money close to the goal line, though, with a quick slant to put 6 on the board. I like seeing him get the timing throws from Nix that allow him to use his frame to protect the catch.

Evan Engram had a pretty active game this week as well. He took a screen for 19 yards right behind a blitz. He ended the day with 4 catches for 33 yards.

Troy Franklin got involved late with a couple of really nice routes for 1st-down completions, with one of them inside the red zone. He caught another 13-yard pass on a curl. It was good to see Franklin step up and make plays with Waddle out. Franklin isn't Waddle, but he produced this week when his number was called.

The defense had some pretty significant struggles off and on throughout this game. As the 4th quarter rolled around, it appeared to me that Bryce Young was going to be able to have success passing all the way down to the wire.

The only way this team was going to be able to win was with some big-time turnovers. Vance Joseph put his players in position to make it work, and they provided the kind of soul-wrenching turnovers that make a fan base want to cry about refs, complain about takebacks, and call your team a bunch of big meanies.

This was a gutsy victory for the Broncos defense. They were already out Kris Abrams-Draine, Talanoa Hufanga, and Brandon Jones to start the game. They lost Riley Moss early and seemed to me to switch mainly to zone calls that kept the defense in front of them which just isn't what this defense is used to doing. It got the job done even though it wasn't pretty.

Many watching the game were complaining about the soft zone calls, but I don't know that you'd like it if we just put in our normal match zone with the group of depth players we had on the field.

Look, the players and coaches talk really big about "Next man up." They talk about how they expect the backups to come in and have no drop-off. That's absolute horse shit, honestly. I'm sorry, but Jahdae Barron is no Riley Moss. Taylor Rapp is no Huff. JL Skinner is no Jones. Devon Key isn't either. These guys are lower down on the depth chart for a reason. Expecting them to be able to press man or match zone in one-on-ones across the board would have been disastrous. The one ace card the Panthers have is a superb young quarterback who knows how to drop dimes. All it takes is one bad half-step by a backup corner or safety, and it would have been 50+ yard touchdowns multiple times.

Don't get me wrong, I hate soft zone looks where your guys are starting 8 yards off their guys and give up pass after pass, just like all of you. The game of NFL football is not so simple that you can just wave a wand and turn a 4th string player into a solid press-man defender.

Feel free to disagree, but my hat is off to Vance Joseph. Great defensive coordinators take a game like this and find a way to get the job done. The players made the plays to get the win. Joseph called the game in a way that put them in a position to make those plays.

Nik Bonitto spent most of the game drawing a lot of attention. Heading late into the 4th quarter, he was only able to chip in a couple of tackles for loss and a quarterback hit. But big players make big plays in big moments. Bonitto absolutely won this game for the Broncos. Young was about to tear this defense a new butthole (he had just done so on the previous drive). All it takes is one big play, though, to seal the deal, and Bonitto is no stranger to being That Guy™.

Jonathon Cooper's presence up front is definitely being felt. He got a half sack in the game, but definitely was collapsing the pocket well from his side fairly constantly. He's always been a tough assignment for any tackle as he brings a ton of power to his bull rush and rarely gets stood up. The stat sheet doesn't always tell the whole story, and I'm just saying I noticed him doing work this game that won't show up with numbers.

The calendar month changed, and with it, Alex Singleton turned back into a pumpkin. He got another 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty for a late hit. He also did a crap job of tackling in the open field, letting a runner get by and move the chains. He bit on a little juke by Young and gave up a big pass when he could have sacked him. He was stacking 10+ tackle games for weeks (kinda normal for him) and had but 6 this game while the team was led in tackles by a corner.

Justin Strnad made a nice open-field tackle in the flat. He had a nice tackle for loss in the game and pass defense.

Devon Key's interception gets him in this review because it was such a momentum-swinging play. His reaction time was very impressive, reaching to snatch the ball before it hit the turf. It ended up being a 13-point swing for the Broncos and easily the key play of the game.

Ja'Quan McMillian made an excellent open-field tackle to get the defense off the field on 3rd down early. He got beat on a corner route in the end zone to give up an easy touchdown. He also got a defensive holding penalty trying to block the tight end who was going out on a passing route. Even so, he was a big player for the Broncos in this game with a big sack late in the 4th quarter when Young couldn't find anyone open fast enough. McMillian also had 2 tackles for loss in the game and a quarterback hit. He's an excellent blitzer, and Vance set him loose a few times in this game to great effect.

Riley Moss dropped another heartbreaker interception that he played perfectly. When he's done shaking off his really scary concussion (he went full boxer posture).

Jahdae Barron had to step in for Moss and immediately got targeted. He made his tackle in the open field with no problem. He gave up a perfectly thrown ball to the sideline and was a full step behind. He also gave up a PI in the end zone, making contact way too early with two arms hugging the tight end. He lined up in off-coverage on 4th and 1 (which is a big mistake either on him or the alignment called for the play) and gave up an easy conversion. I wasn't really impressed with Barron's play in this game. I'm not sure if he's cut out to stay at corner in the NFL or if he's better off transitioning to safety.

Patrick Surtain had an uncharacteristically rough game. He gave up a 3rd and 17 with uncharacteristic flat-footed, slow-reaction coverage. He also got beat for an easy touchdown late in the 4th quarter.

JL Skinner gave up a deep crosser to start the 2nd half. He also gave up a deep post for a touchdown at the end of the drive.

Jeremy Crawshaw put together another impressive punting game with a net average of 45 yards per punt, with one of his 3 downed inside the 20. Hopefully he enjoys flowing beer and his share of chundering this bye week if he's into that sort of thing.

Nate Adkins straight-up leveled some fool on a return late in the game, and I think the returner's children are going to feel that hit.

At this point, I honestly feel like any opponent we face is going to be at an automatic disadvantage in any game that they aren't winning by 3 scores headed into the 4th quarter. The Broncos' aura has grown to blinding proportions when it comes to one-score games.

They were supposed to regress to the mean. They were supposed to take a big step back this year facing a 1st-place schedule.

Sean Payton's Broncos do not give two hoots about what people say they are "supposed" to do. Give them a 1st-place schedule with a 6-game gauntlet from hell to start the season and 9 games before they get a bye week.

They will see you at the break at 7-2, sitting pretty while the talking heads are still wondering how they win anything with a noodle-armed quarterback who only checks down and is plainly just terrible at everything (this is called "sarcasm", ladies and gentlemen).

#2884. Hull City's Oli McBurnie opens up on emotional Scotland return under Pocognoli

Striker Oli McBurnie has recalled the deeply personal moment he received the call from new Scotland manager Sébastien Pocognoli, confirming his international comeback after five years in exile.

The Hull City forward had nearly abandoned hopes of ending his international drought under previous head coach Steve Clarke, despite netting 19 goals for the Tigers, including the crucial Wembley goal that secured the club's Premier League promotion, having been overlooked for the World Cup.

McBurnie concluded his club commitments on Saturday following the Tigers' tight 1-0 defeat at Arsenal, with focus now shifting to two pivotal Nations League fixtures at home against North Macedonia on Friday night, before traveling to Switzerland on Monday evening.

Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac address Wrexham executive's abrupt exit

USMNT legend Alexi Lalas on Mauricio Pochettino to Man Utd links amidst pressure on Michael Carrick

"He (Pocognoli) FaceTimed me; he messaged me, asking if I was free," the City forward recalls in conversation with Hull Live. "I was just sat at home with the kids and the missus, and he FaceTimed me out of the blue and told me about his plans and what he'd been watching and what he'd seen in me and what he'd wanted his teams to be and them sort of thing.

"We had a good chat, and then he told me that I was going to be in. It was, it was hard for me to keep the smile off my face, and yeah, it was, it was a really nice moment.", reports Hull Live.

Make sure you never miss the latest Hull City news and opinion by making Hull Live one of your Google preferred sources. "He's (Pocognoli) been brilliant. While we were away, I learnt a lot about him. The thing is, with internationals, they have so little time to implement their game plan. You have 25 lads coming from 25 different teams that all play a different way, and then you have a week of training. It's gonna take time, but yeah, I was really impressed with the manager and his ideas, and yeah, really impressed.

"My missus was in the room with the kids, so she heard it, so I didn't have to tell them because they heard it. I was trying to tell my little one; she didn't quite get it. She knows Hull as the Tigers cos she likes tigers, and Scotland has a lion on it, so the Lions. That's the way she knows. They came up, watched the games that were at Hampden.

"All the things now that you do is for your kids, so my kids have been able to see me represent my country. It was something I never thought they'd get to see. I've played however many times for Scotland before, and it was something that I never thought they'd get to see their old man playing for the country. To get to see their old man playing in the Premier League and playing for his country as well. It was nice for me and for them to see that."

McBurnie featured in all four of Scotland's Nations League fixtures during the revamped international window earlier this campaign, though he acknowledges feeling disappointed at failing to score and finally get off the mark after 20 caps and over 1,000 minutes on the pitch.

"Oh it was good, mate, it was really good. You know how long it's been for me, and how long it's been a goal for me to get back into the team, so I loved it," he continued. "I probably should have had a couple of goals, but the gaffer giving me the chance, I started all four games when I was up there in a little bit of a different position, but really enjoyed it being back with the lads.

"The skip (ex-City man Andy Robertson) had his 100th appearance while I was away with him as well, so seeing things like that and being back involved with the Scotland setup, it's a real proud one."

While McBurnie may have been a familiar returnee, he notes the influx of fresh faces in the squad helped ease the anxiety of coming back after a five year absence.

"I did feel like a little bit like a kid on the first day of school," the 30 year old admitted. "I knew half of the boys from the last time, but what helped was there was another set of new lads, like seven or eight, that had never been in there for the first time, so I was more experienced than them, even though I was still kind of one of the newbies. It was good.

"It was nervy for the first couple of days, but the gaffer was brilliant, and whatever happens now, I'll always be grateful to him for giving me that chance to represent my country."

Sergej Jakirovic lightheartedly suggested that McBurnie was frustrated at missing out on his golf during the international break, to which McBurnie fired back that a broken finger had already ruled out any such plans regardless.

"My finger has done me in anyway, so there's no golf for me at the minute, so it's kind of a bit easier. I haven't played golf for a while; maybe that's why I ain't scored so many. I haven't been playing my golf, but no, it's tough, and the weather's getting a bit worse now anyway, so it might be club's away for the winter now."

#2883. Stats Rundown: 4 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 125-122 comeback win over the Pacers

The Dallas Mavericks (7-4) were on the second night of a back-to-back when they welcomed the Indiana Pacers (3-8) Monday night. They found themselves battling back from a deficit for most of the first half, but in the third quarter they started to find a groove and ultimately pulled away for a 125-122 win in a game that came down to the final possession. Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving led the way, while players like Walter Clayton, Santi Aldama and Caleb Martin did the little things around the edges for what proved to be a total team victory.

The duo of Flagg and Irving is absolutely terrifying when they are "on" and they were on Monday night. The pair dropped 78 points combined on impressive efficiency. Together, they shot 27-of-43, good for a 62.7% connection rate. Irving hit an insane 7-of-10 from downtown, with Flagg an excellent 3-of-6 in his own right. They were also 14-of-15 from the free throw line. Each player individually was a sight to behold, but the combination of what they were doing together was truly next level.

A single game plus/minus needs to be looked at carefully, as it can be misleading. Having said that, Irving played 38 minutes and was a game-high +29 with no other player on either team being even close (the next best was +15 by Daniel Gafford and Andrew Nembhard). Irving's presence was apparent from his scoring, but he did so much more than that as a poised floor general that helped the Mavs to victory in other ways as well.

Don't look now, but Dallas once again dominated on the boards. Being +16 on the glass in a three-point game is unquestionably a big factor in why the Mavs came out on top. The best part of the disparity is that Gafford was in foul trouble most of the night and Morez Johnson, Jr. sat out altogether. Within the overall discrepancy was Dallas' 10-1 offensive rebound advantage.

On the final possession with the Mavericks up by three points, the Pacers were inbounding from half-court. Dusty May substituted Irving for Martin for his length and defensive prowess and Martin rewarded him and Mavs nation with the defensive stop of the night. On a somewhat errant pass across nearly the entire court sideline-to-sideline, Martin streaked in and tipped the ball away from Pascal Siakam, allowing the clock to run out. Pacers' coach Rick Carlisle was furious there was no foul call, however it appeared to be the correct no-call by the referees. Martin got his hand on the ball and tipped it well away from Siakam before the two players' body's made contact with each other. As a result, the Pacers weren't able to attempt a final shot and Dallas got the win.
